  Line 7: TiN NPs are not always compatible with projected biomedical applications. Indeed, chemical synthesis routes24,25 

  Line 8: are rather complicated in terms of a number of preparation steps and employ hazardous products, which can 

  Line 9: cause residual contamination of NPs and related toxicity issues. On the other hand, nanocrystals prepared by 

  Line 10: dry fabrication methods, including direct nitridation of TiO

  Line 11: 2 powders26, plasma assisted processing27–29 and laser 

  Line 12: ablation in nitrogen atmosphere 17, normally cannot be dispersed and stabilized in aqueous solutions without 

  Line 13: applying similar wet chemistry steps.

  Line 14: Here, we demonstrate a simple and cost efficient method for the production of stable solutions of bare (ligand –  

  Line 15: free) TiN NPs by methods of femtosecond (fs) laser ablation and fragmentation in water and organic (acetone) 

  Line 16: solutions. By performing a series of biological tests using 2D cultures and 3D spheroids, we evidence high safety 

  Line 17: and excellent cell uptake of laser-synthesized TiN NPs, as well as show efficient therapy effect on cancer cells using 

  Line 18: TiN NPs as sensitizers of photothermal treatment at the plasmonic absorption band (650–800 nm).

  Line 20: synthesis and characterization of t iN nanoparticles.  For the synthesis of TiN NPs we adapted 

  Line 21: methods of ultra-short laser ablation and fragmentation in liquid ambience, which were earlier used for the 

  Line 22: preparation of bare Au and Ag NPs

  Line 23: 30–36. In the first “ablation” approach30–32, radiation from a femtosecond laser 

  Line 24: (Yb:KGW , 1025 nm, 1–100 kHz) was focused onto a TiN target placed on the bottom of a glass vessel filled with 

  Line 25: deionized water or acetone in order to initiate ablation of material, as shown in Fig.  1a (see details in Methods 

  Line 26: section). The target was continuously moved at a speed of 2 mm s− 1 during the ablation step to avoid ablation 

  Line 27: from the same point.

  Line 28: We observed a blue coloration of solution within a few minutes of the ablation process, indicating the for -

  Line 29: mation of TiN NPs. Concentration of NPs increased linearly at the beginning of the process and then came to 

  Line 30: a saturation after some time. Saturation concentration and time until saturation depended on pulse energy. In 

  Line 31: particular, for 100 μJ pulse energy and 5 kHz repetition rate saturation time was 15 min and the saturation con-

  Line 35: months. Such a high stability of colloidal solutions was due to an electrostatic stabilization owing to strong charg-

  Line 36: ing of NPs surface similar to how it happens for other materials

  Line 37: 33. Indeed, according to our ζ–potential measure-

  Line 38: ments, the surface potential of TiN NPs was − 30 mV , which is higher than the stability threshold (20 mV)37 for

  Line 40: A typical HR-TEM image of a TiN nanoparticle synthesized by pulsed laser ablation in water is shown in 

  Line 41: Fig. 2a. One can see that the nanoparticle had a spherical shape and exhibited a polycrystalline structure, while 

  Line 42: the size of single-crystal grains was about 1–3 nm. Interestingly, TiN NPs could have a hollow structure con-

  Line 45: ambient the relevant parameter could reach 60%. Moreover, most of hollow NPs had only one cavity under ace-

  Line 46: tone conditions, while under water conditions they could contain several cavities. As another observation, when 

  Line 47: ablated in acetone, all synthesized TiN NPs were spherical and crystalline, while the ablation in water ambient 

  Line 48: was accompanied by the production of a certain amount of nanostructured amorphous flakes. Based on our pre-

  Line 56: TiN, should belong to titanium oxide fraction of synthesized NPs. In particular, position of ring 1 is close to that

  Line 58: 2O3 (JCPDS 43-1033), the position of ring 5 is close to (105) plane of anatase TiO2 and (211) 

  Line 59: plane of rutile TiO2 (JCPDS 21-1272 and 21-1276). Thus, SAED data clearly indicated formation of crystalline 

  Line 60: TiN NPs with lattice structure similar to that of bulk TiN with some fraction of titanium oxide. Presence of 

  Line 61: titanium oxide is in accordance with previous results on the synthesis of TiN NPs by alternative methods

  Line 62: 20,23,25.

  Line 65: particular, the increase of pulse energy from 10 to 100 μJ led to the increase of NPs mean diameter from 25 to 

  Line 66: 40 nm under relatively broad size dispersion (25–40 nm FWHM). Such a pulse energy dependence for the mean 

  Line 67: size of TiN NPs is in agreement with our previous data on fs laser ablation of Au in deionized water30,31. For abla-

  Line 68: tion in water, the dependence of NPs size on pulse energy was not significant and the mean size of synthesized 

  Line 69: TiN NPs was always around 30 nm under the size dispersion of 40 nm FWHM. It is important that TiN NPs pre-

  Line 74: centrifugation step.

  Line 75: To further reduce the mean size and narrow down size dispersion, we employed the technique of femtosecond
